liturgical_day: Friday of the Twenty-third Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: Clear sight begins within
theme: Jesus forms disciples who learn from him, examine themselves honestly, and correct others only with purified sight.
introduction: Jesus joins guidance, discipleship, and correction into one searching lesson. A blind guide cannot lead another safely, because counsel requires a life illuminated by truth. The disciple therefore remains beneath the Master, receiving Christ's teaching until it takes visible form in character. Only then can correction become service rather than self-display. The speck and the beam expose how readily the eye turns outward while remaining unaware of its own obstruction. Christ does not forbid every attempt to help a brother; his final words envision the speck being removed. He commands an order: repentance first, then clear-sighted assistance. The person who confronts his own grave faults can approach another without hypocrisy, superiority, or the dangerous blindness that sends both guide and guided into the ditch.
hero_alt: Jesus teaches disciples on a Galilean plain about clear sight, humble self-examination, and compassionate guidance in Byzantine mosaic and stained glass
closing_title: Let Christ clear the guide's vision
closing: Before offering correction today, stand first as a disciple before Christ. Ask where anger, vanity, fear, or an unexamined habit may be distorting your sight. Name the beam without excuse and bring it to repentance, prayer, and whatever concrete amendment it requires. This humility does not make loving guidance impossible; it makes guidance trustworthy. Christ's warning is directed especially toward anyone responsible for another, yet every disciple influences companions by word and example. We cannot lead beyond the truth we ourselves refuse to follow. Stay close to the Master, whose mercy exposes sin in order to heal it. When he clears the eye, a brother's speck is no longer an occasion for superiority. It becomes a call to patient, truthful assistance from one person who needs mercy to another.

verses.text: And he also spoke a parable to them: Can the blind lead the blind? Do they not both fall into the ditch?
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril applies the parable first to those who will teach. A guide must receive divine light and embody a virtuous life, or both teacher and hearer are endangered.
verses.commentary: Cyril says this parable was especially necessary because the disciples were to become teachers of the world. Those charged with guiding others must know the path of virtue themselves, with minds enlightened by divine brightness. Otherwise they remain blind while attempting to lead the blind, and both are carried toward the same fall. Christian teaching therefore cannot be separated from the teacher's conversion. Knowledge that has not illuminated conduct is insufficient for safe guidance. The disciple must first receive Christ's light and walk by it before directing another person's steps.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:39–42

verses.text: A disciple is not above his master; but everyone shall be perfect if he is like his master.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede points to Christ's patient mercy as the Master's rule of perfection. The disciple is formed by imitating him rather than claiming a harsher authority.
verses.commentary: Bede connects the disciple's perfection with the pattern already shown by Christ. Although the Master possesses divine authority and could avenge the injuries done to him, he chose patience in order to draw his persecutors toward mercy. A disciple cannot claim to stand above that example. Human weakness is not permission to judge more harshly than Christ; it is a reason to follow his patience more closely. Formation is complete when the pupil resembles the Master. Christian maturity therefore appears not in severity or superiority, but in a life shaped by Christ's merciful way of confronting evil.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:39–42

verses.text: And why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but do not consider the beam in your own eye?
verses.author: St Basil the Great
verses.insight: Basil identifies self-knowledge as indispensable. The mind notices another's fault quickly while remaining strangely slow to recognize its own defects.
verses.commentary: Basil observes that self-knowledge is among the most important of all attainments. The bodily eye looks outward and cannot naturally turn its sight upon itself; the understanding often behaves in the same way. It can be keen and rapid when detecting another person's sin, yet sluggish when asked to perceive its own faults. Christ's contrast between speck and beam exposes this imbalance. The problem is not careful moral perception itself, but perception directed everywhere except inward. Honest examination restores proportion, because it brings our own need for purification into view before we scrutinize a brother.
verses.source_label: St Basil the Great, Homily 9 on the Hexaemeron, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:39–42

verses.text: Or how can you say to your brother, 'Brother, let me pull the speck out of your eye,' when you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye; and then you shall see clearly to take the speck from your brother's eye.
verses.author: Theophylact of Ohrid
verses.insight: Theophylact sees hypocrisy when correction hides uncorrected sin. Christ requires purification first, so that counsel becomes clear-sighted help rather than a performance of righteousness.
verses.commentary: Theophylact applies Christ's warning to everyone, and especially to teachers who punish small faults in those entrusted to them while leaving their own serious sins untouched. Such correction becomes hypocritical because attention to another's failure is used to create an appearance of personal righteousness. Jesus does not end by abandoning the brother with the speck. He commands the would-be guide first to cast out the beam, and only then to help. Repentance gives correction its proper order and purpose. Purified sight can offer counsel humbly, without using another person's weakness to conceal or excuse one's own.
verses.source_label: Theophylact of Ohrid, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:39–42
